Sore
sōr
adv. and adj. (grievously, severely; rendering Hebrew me'od and gadol, Greek sphodra)
From Saxon sar, painful or grievous. In the Authorized Version it is chiefly an adverb of degree meaning grievously or severely — not the modern noun for a wound. Sore afraid, sore vexed, and sore broken are its standing phrases.

Biblical Definition

Sore in the Authorized Version usually means grievously or severely, an adverb of degree rather than the modern noun. Its commonest phrase is sore afraid: Abimelech, warned in a dream that he has taken another man's wife, tells his servants, and “the men were sore afraid” (Genesis 20:8). It measures the weight of God's hand in chastening: “For thine arrows stick fast in me, and thy hand presseth me sore” (Psalm 38:2), where David does not soften the description of a discipline he acknowledges to be deserved. It measures the guilt of a king: Ahaz “made Judah naked, and transgressed sore against the LORD” (2 Chronicles 28:19). And Ecclesiastes uses it as an adjective for an evil observed under the sun: “There is a sore evil which I have seen under the sun, namely, riches kept for the owners thereof to their hurt” (Ecclesiastes 5:13) — wealth hoarded until it damages the man who holds it, which the Preacher classes among the grievous things.

Webster 1828 Definition

An adverb and adjective meaning grievously, severely, or painful. In Scripture chiefly adverbial — sore afraid, presseth me sore, transgressed sore — measuring the degree of fear, of chastening, or of guilt.

expand to see more

SORE, a. [Sax. sar.] Painful; tender to the touch; as, a sore wound.

2. Grievous; severe; violent; as, a sore famine, a sore evil.

3. SORE, adv. Greatly; violently; severely; as, sore afraid, sore vexed.

4. SORE, n. A place in an animal body where the skin and flesh are bruised or broken.

5. In Scripture, the men were sore afraid, Gen. 20; thy hand presseth me sore, Psa. 38.

Key Scripture

Genesis 20:8 — "Therefore Abimelech rose early in the morning, and called all his servants, and told all these things in their ears: and the men were sore afraid."

Psalm 38:2 — "For thine arrows stick fast in me, and thy hand presseth me sore."

2 Chronicles 28:19 — "For the LORD brought Judah low because of Ahaz king of Israel; for he made Judah naked, and transgressed sore against the LORD."

Ecclesiastes 5:13 — "There is a sore evil which I have seen under the sun, namely, riches kept for the owners thereof to their hurt."

Modern Corruption

The Preacher's sore evil — riches kept by their owners to their own hurt — is not a warning against wealth but against hoarding, and it names the damage as falling first on the man who hoards.

expand to see more

Ecclesiastes is not teaching that property is wrong. Scripture establishes and protects it, commends diligence, and honours the man who leaves an inheritance to his children's children. What the Preacher observes is a particular ruin: wealth held, watched, and never used, until the holding itself becomes the injury — sleeplessness, suspicion, and finally a loss in which nothing remains for the son. The rich fool of Luke 12 is the same man in a parable, pulling down barns to build greater ones on the night his soul is required of him.

The biblical remedy is not asceticism but liberality. Paul's charge to the rich is exact and worth stating in full: that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy; that they do good, that they be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate. Notice that enjoyment is commanded as well as giving. Between the ascetic who despises God's gifts and the miser who cannot release them stands the steward, who both uses and distributes what was never finally his.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew intensifies with me'od (very, exceedingly) and gadol (great); the phrase yare' me'od gives sore afraid. Greek uses sphodra, exceedingly. The Saxon sar means painful or grievous.

expand to see more

Hebrew me'od (H3966) — very, exceedingly, greatly; the standard intensive rendered sore.

Hebrew yare' (H3372) — to fear, to be afraid; with me'od it gives the phrase sore afraid.

Hebrew ra'ah cholah (H7451, H2470) — a sick or grievous evil; the sore evil of Ecclesiastes 5:13.

Greek sphodra (G4970) — exceedingly, greatly; the New Testament intensive of the same force.

Saxon sar — painful, grievous; the root of both the adverb and the modern noun.

Usage

"Of great fear at a divine warning: and the men were sore afraid (Genesis 20:8)."

"Of chastening acknowledged as heavy and deserved: thy hand presseth me sore (Psalm 38:2)."

"Of wealth hoarded to the owner's hurt: There is a sore evil which I have seen under the sun (Ecclesiastes 5:13)."
